title: Same lists, one switch
hook: Same four rankings, same rules. Swap who makes the offers and the outcome changes.

knows: ranking options from first to last
doesNotKnow: that in a matching market who proposes decides who gets their first choice
that deferred acceptance always ends stable

misconception: A stable matching procedure is neutral between the two sides.
objective: The learner can explain that the same rankings give different stable matchings depending on which side proposes, and that the proposing side gets its best stable partner.

claims.text: With Ann ranking X then Y, Bea Y then X, X ranking Bea then Ann, and Y ranking Ann then Bea, students proposing gives Ann-X and Bea-Y, and both students get their first choice.
claims.source: Builder's node script of deferred acceptance (students propose): Ann offers X, Bea offers Y, no offer is refused. Matching Ann-X, Bea-Y; Ann's and Bea's first choices; both hospitals get their second choice.

claims.text: With the same rankings, hospitals proposing gives X-Bea and Y-Ann, and both hospitals get their first choice.
claims.source: Builder's node script (hospitals propose): X offers Bea, Y offers Ann, no refusals. Matching Bea-X, Ann-Y; X's and Y's first choices; both students get their second choice.

claims.text: Both matchings are stable: no student and hospital both prefer each other to their partners. In the students' matching (Ann-X, Bea-Y), Ann would not swap to Y and Bea would not swap to X (Y and X would); in the hospitals' matching (X-Bea, Y-Ann), X would not swap to Ann and Y would not swap to Bea (Ann and Bea would).
claims.source: Builder's node check of all student-hospital pairs against both matchings (the stage log also computes it): no blocking pair in either. Each side that is not at its first choice would have to move to a partner that already has a better one. | REVISED v3 (demo-builder, 2026-10-14): v3 shows the check on stage: 'Would a pair rather swap?' prints e.g. 'Swap? Ann–Y: Ann no, Y yes. Bea–X: Bea no, X yes. No double yes: stable.' for each finished run, computed by swapRows/isStable in Demo.tsx; the reveal quotes who said no. Unverified. | FC pass 24 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): Own node check of both 2 x 2 matchings against the rankings: students' (Ann-X, Bea-Y): Ann-Y Ann no / Y yes, Bea-X Bea no / X yes; hospitals' (X-Bea, Y-Ann): Ann-X Ann yes / X no, Bea-Y Bea yes / Y no; 0 blocking pairs in each. In this 2 x 2 no offer is ever refused, so each mode has one outcome whatever the press order. v3 check line and reveal (whoSaysNo from the recorded check, milestone checked-both requires both) print exactly these yes/no values; the switch keeps the log and checks.

claims.text: Deferred acceptance always ends stable and gives the proposing side its best stable partner.
claims.source: Gale and Shapley 1962, College admissions and the stability of marriage, Amer. Math. Monthly 69(1), theorems 1 and 2 (proposer-optimality).

claims.text: The US residency match switched to students proposing in 1998, a change studied by Roth and Peranson (1999).
claims.source: Roth and Peranson 1999, The redesign of the matching market for American physicians, Amer. Econ. Rev. 89(4). Check the 'for this reason' wording against the paper: the redesign adopted an applicant-proposing algorithm; the paper discusses applicant-optimality as a motive. | v2 (2026-10-14, builder): motive ("for this reason") dropped per pass 19; the claim now asserts only the 1998 switch to applicant-proposing and that Roth and Peranson (1999) studied it. Year 1998 and the paper not opened by the builder (from the pass-19 fix wording and the paper title). Previous verdict void; needs re-check. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 20): Demo.tsx reveal line 211 matches claim text. Year: primary pages unreachable this pass (stanford.edu, nrmp.org, natmatch.com, AER all blocked); corroborated by search results quoting Roth's Stanford NRMP page (board voted 5 May 1997 to adopt the new algorithm), Wikipedia (first applied March 1998), an NRMP press release of 8 May 1997 (change effective 1998) and medschoolinsiders (first used in the March 1998 Match). claims.text: In this example no offer is ever refused, so each person gets one of their two choices on a single offer.
claims.source: Builder's node trace: both runs end after two offers with no refusals. Stage behaviour for refusals (receiver keeps the better offer, loser's line struck) is built but not on the QA path. Not shown to the learner as text.

recall.question: Two sides each rank the other. Running deferred acceptance twice on the same rankings, once with each side proposing, can give two different stable matchings. Which side does better in its own run?
recall.why: Deferred acceptance gives the proposing side its best stable partner, so switching who proposes can change who is happy.
